subsystems.role: reads the measurement outcomes of ancilla qubits that flag errors without collapsing the data qubits.

subsystems.name: Decoder algorithm core
subsystems.role: turns a stream of syndromes into a guess at which physical errors occurred.

subsystems.name: Classical processing fabric
subsystems.role: runs the decoder fast enough to keep up with the quantum computer.

subsystems.name: Feedback and control path
subsystems.role: applies corrections to the live quantum computation before errors spread.

subsystems.name: Calibration and validation
subsystems.role: keeps the decoder matched to the machine's actual noise.

buildSteps.title: Choose the quantum error-correcting code
buildSteps.detail: Most designs use a surface code or a related topological code, which defines what a syndrome means and how errors must be corrected.

buildSteps.title: Model the noise
buildSteps.detail: Error rates for each gate and measurement are measured on the real hardware, because the decoder's accuracy depends on this model.

buildSteps.title: Design the decoder algorithm
buildSteps.detail: A graph-based method such as minimum-weight perfect matching or union-find is chosen for its speed and accuracy; neural decoders are researched as alternatives.

buildSteps.title: Map it onto classical hardware
buildSteps.detail: The algorithm is rewritten into parallel, pipelined logic for FPGAs, or laid out as an ASIC when volumes justify the cost.

buildSteps.title: Meet the latency budget
buildSteps.detail: The decoder must return a correction within the coherence time of the qubits, often under a microsecond, which sets how much parallelism and memory bandwidth are needed.

buildSteps.title: Integrate with the quantum control stack
buildSteps.detail: The decoder is wired into the same real-time electronics that drive the qubits, so syndromes arrive and corrections leave in step with the experiment.

buildSteps.title: Validate in simulation and on hardware
buildSteps.detail: Decoders are first tested against simulated noise, then run on small real quantum processors to check that logical error rates fall as expected.

buildSteps.title: Scale to many qubits
buildSteps.detail: Larger codes need decoder instances running in parallel, with careful partitioning so that communication does not become the bottleneck.

prerequisites.why: surface and related codes are well understood in theory and are now run on small hardware.

prerequisites.tech: Qubits with error rates below the code threshold
prerequisites.why: below-threshold operation has been shown in small experiments, but not yet at the scale of a useful computation.
these devices can implement graph decoders with sub-microsecond latency in laboratory demonstrations.

prerequisites.tech: Low-latency cryogenic or room-temperature control electronics
prerequisites.why: signals must move between the cryogenic quantum chip and the decoder without introducing delays that break the correction cycle.
the decoder must be synchronised with pulse-level control, which is still an active engineering problem.

pathway.milestone: real-time decoding demonstrated on small surface-code experiments
pathway.unlocks: proof that correction can keep pace with a handful of logical qubits.

pathway.milestone: decoders scaled to hundreds of qubits with FPGA clusters
pathway.unlocks: logical qubits that live long enough for early algorithms.

pathway.milestone: ASIC decoders with tight integration to cryogenic control
pathway.unlocks: the latency and power needed for thousands of qubits.

pathway.milestone: fault-tolerant logical processors with thousands of logical qubits
pathway.unlocks: practical quantum computing for chemistry, materials and cryptography.
